The magic numbers are 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, and 126, a pattern that is similar to one that identifies the stable closed shells of atoms, 2, 10, 18, 36, etc. Examples of nuclei with magic numbers of protons include the isotopes of He, O, Ca, and Ni, with Z 5 2, 8, 20, and 28, respectively. Isotopes with magic numbers of neutrons are also magic; examples include 36S, 37C, and 38Ar. Isotopes with magic numbers of both protons and neutrons are called “doubly magic” nuclei, and they are excep- tionally stable. The best known examples are 2He 4 and 8O 16 , but others include

20Ca 40 , 20Ca 48 , and 28Ni 48 . The last two are particularly interesting examples of the influence of magic numbers on stability. 20Ca 48 is a very neutron-rich light nucleus that we would predict not to be very stable, based upon considerations discussed earlier, but it has a half-life of the order of 1020 years and is considered stable for all practical purposes. 28Ni 48 , on the other hand, lying at the extreme end of the proton-rich nuclei with A 5 48, was not thought to exist at all, though it has been discovered recently but with a very short half-life. The stability of the 2He 4 nucleus, the a particle, is particularly striking; its binding energy per nucleon is equivalent to those of the heavier elements, because it is a doubly magic nucleus. The excep- tional stability of the  particle accounts for the important role it plays in nuclear decay processes. Losing an  particle reduces the Coulomb repulsion between pro- tons, which increases the stability of the daughter nuclide, without affecting the average binding energy per nucleon.
